title: Reading a Menu and Food Vocabulary
objectives: Read and interpret American restaurant menus including descriptions, categories, and pricing
Identify and use food vocabulary for common American and international dishes
Distinguish between countable and uncountable nouns when describing food
Describe food using sensory adjectives related to taste, texture, and preparation method

reading_passage.title: Understanding What You're Ordering
reading_passage.text:
For newcomers eating out in the United States, menus can be both exciting and confusing. American menus often include dishes from many different culinary traditions — Italian pasta, Mexican tacos, Japanese sushi, and American classics like mac and cheese or chicken wings — all available in the same restaurant. Understanding how dishes are described helps you order confidently and avoid surprises.

Most menus describe dishes using sensory language. Words like 'crispy,' 'tender,' 'grilled,' 'smoked,' 'braised,' and 'sautéed' describe how food is cooked. Words like 'creamy,' 'tangy,' 'savoury,' 'mild,' and 'rich' describe how food tastes. Reading these descriptions carefully can tell you a great deal about whether a dish will suit your preferences and dietary needs.

One source of confusion is the difference between countable and uncountable food nouns. 'A burger,' 'two tacos,' and 'three eggs' are countable — you can order a specific number of them. But 'rice,' 'bread,' 'pasta,' 'soup,' and 'coffee' are uncountable — you cannot say 'two rices' or 'a soup' in standard English. Instead, you use quantifiers: 'a bowl of soup,' 'a cup of coffee,' 'a serving of rice,' or 'a slice of bread.'

Menus also often note which dishes contain common allergens — nuts, dairy, gluten, or shellfish — using small icons or asterisks. If you have a dietary restriction or allergy, it is always safer to confirm with the server rather than relying only on the menu description.
reading_passage.source: Adapted from ESL food literacy curriculum developed by Oregon Literacy Inc. and Portland Community College Continuing Education, 2023

glossary.meaning: relating to cooking and food preparation
cooked slowly in a small amount of liquid in a covered pot, resulting in tender, flavourful meat
cooked quickly in a small amount of oil or butter over high heat
a substance in food that can cause an allergic reaction in some people, such as nuts, dairy, or gluten
a word that indicates the amount or quantity of something, such as 'a cup of,' 'some,' or 'a few'

comprehension.question: According to the passage, what do words like 'crispy,' 'grilled,' and 'braised' describe on a menu?
comprehension.answer: They describe how food is cooked — the preparation method used to make the dish.

comprehension.question: Why does the author advise confirming allergen information with the server rather than relying only on the menu?
comprehension.answer: Because menus can be incomplete or unclear — icons and asterisks may be easy to miss, and a server can give specific, up-to-date information about ingredients to ensure the meal is safe for someone with allergies.

comprehension.question: What does 'culinary' mean in the first paragraph?
comprehension.answer: Relating to cooking and food preparation — a 'culinary tradition' refers to the food practices and recipes that come from a particular culture or country.

comprehension.question: What does the author imply by saying that many different food traditions appear on the same American restaurant menu?
comprehension.answer: The author implies that American food culture is diverse and internationally influenced — and that this variety, while exciting, can be unfamiliar and even overwhelming for newcomers who are still learning English food vocabulary.

language_focus.title: Countable and Uncountable Nouns with Food
language_focus.explanation: Food nouns in English are either countable (you can count individual items: one egg, two tacos, three cookies) or uncountable (you cannot count them directly: rice, soup, bread, coffee). Uncountable nouns do not take 'a/an' and cannot be pluralised. To express quantity with uncountable nouns, use a quantifier phrase: 'a bowl of soup,' 'a cup of coffee,' 'a piece of bread,' 'a serving of rice.' Getting this right sounds natural and helps when ordering food.

examples.sentence: Could I have a bowl of rice and two pieces of flatbread, please?
examples.note: 'Rice' and 'bread' are uncountable — use 'a bowl of rice' and 'pieces of bread,' not 'a rice' or 'two breads.'

examples.sentence: I'd like three tacos and a glass of water.
examples.note: 'Tacos' and 'glass' are countable — you can say 'three tacos' directly. 'Water' is uncountable, so use 'a glass of water.'

practice.sentence: Correct the error: 'Can I have a soup and two breads, please?'
practice.answer: Can I have a bowl of soup and two slices of bread, please? (Use quantifiers with uncountable nouns: 'a bowl of soup,' 'slices of bread.')

practice.sentence: Choose the correct form: 'I'd like ___ (a coffee / a cup of coffee) to start.'
practice.answer: I'd like a cup of coffee to start. ('Coffee' is uncountable — use 'a cup of coffee,' not 'a coffee' in formal restaurant language.)

practice.sentence: Which nouns are countable? A) rice, pasta, bread. B) egg, taco, sandwich.
practice.answer: B) Egg, taco, and sandwich are countable — you can say 'two eggs,' 'three tacos,' 'one sandwich.' Rice, pasta, and bread are uncountable.

vocabulary_in_context.definition: Relating to cooking, food preparation, and the traditions of making and serving food
vocabulary_in_context.example_sentence: American menus often include dishes from many different culinary traditions — Italian pasta, Mexican tacos, Japanese sushi.

vocabulary_in_context.definition: A substance in food that triggers an allergic reaction in some people, such as nuts, dairy, gluten, or shellfish
vocabulary_in_context.example_sentence: Menus often note which dishes contain common allergens — nuts, dairy, gluten, or shellfish — using small icons or asterisks.

vocabulary_in_context.definition: A word or phrase that shows the amount of something, used before uncountable nouns (a cup of, a bowl of, a piece of)
vocabulary_in_context.example_sentence: Instead, you use quantifiers: 'a bowl of soup,' 'a cup of coffee,' 'a serving of rice,' or 'a slice of bread.'

speaking_task.context: You are helping a newly arrived friend understand a restaurant menu for the first time. The menu has the following items: grilled chicken with a side of rice ($16), tomato bisque soup ($8), beef tacos — three per order ($12), macaroni and cheese ($10), and chocolate lava cake ($7).
speaking_task.prompt: Explain at least three dishes on the menu to your friend. For each one, describe what it is, how it is cooked (if the menu says), and whether any part of it is countable or uncountable. Help your friend choose something they would enjoy based on their preferences.
useful_language: The grilled chicken comes with a serving of rice — 'rice' is uncountable so you can't say 'rices.'
The tacos are countable — you get three in one order, so you can say 'three tacos.'
The tomato bisque is a smooth, creamy soup — 'soup' is uncountable, so you'd ask for 'a bowl of soup.'
speaking_task.model_answer: OK, let me help you read the menu. The grilled chicken is chicken cooked over a flame — 'grilled' means cooked on a grill. It comes with rice on the side. Rice is uncountable, so we say 'a serving of rice,' not 'a rice.' The tacos are small filled tortillas — they're countable, and this order gives you three. The tomato bisque is a smooth creamy soup. Soup is uncountable, so you'd order 'a bowl of soup.' If you prefer something familiar, the macaroni and cheese is pasta with a creamy cheese sauce — very popular here. What do you think you'd like?

writing_workshop.model_text: American menus can seem overwhelming at first, but once you understand the vocabulary, ordering becomes easier. I have learned that 'grilled' means cooked on an open flame, which gives food a slightly smoky taste. 'Braised' means slow-cooked in liquid, which makes meat very tender. When I see 'a bowl of soup' or 'a cup of coffee' on the menu, I now know these are uncountable nouns with quantifiers. My favourite thing to order is grilled salmon with a side of rice — it is light, healthy, and always well cooked. I always ask the server whether any dish contains dairy, since I avoid it.
writing_workshop.model_analysis: Notice how the writer uses food vocabulary learned in the lesson (grilled, braised, uncountable nouns), includes personal experience, and demonstrates how to ask about dietary needs — showing both language and practical knowledge.
writing_workshop.task: Write a description of two or three dishes that you enjoy or would like to try. Describe how they are cooked, what they taste like, and identify whether the main ingredients are countable or uncountable. Include a sentence about any dietary preferences or restrictions you have.
success_criteria: Describe at least two dishes using preparation method words (grilled, baked, fried, etc.) and taste adjectives
Correctly use countable and uncountable nouns — use quantifiers where needed
Include a sentence about a dietary preference or how you would customise an order

quiz.question: According to the passage, what do words like 'creamy,' 'tangy,' and 'mild' describe on a menu?
options: The portion size of the dish
The country the dish comes from
quiz.explanation: The passage states: 'Words like creamy, tangy, savoury, mild, and rich describe how food tastes.'

quiz.question: Which of the following food nouns is uncountable?
quiz.explanation: Rice is uncountable — you cannot say 'two rices.' You must use a quantifier: 'a serving of rice' or 'a bowl of rice.' Taco, egg, and sandwich are countable.

quiz.question: Which sentence correctly uses a quantifier with an uncountable noun?
options: Can I have two soups, please?
Can I have a soup, please?
Can I have a bowl of soup, please?
Can I have some soup bowls, please?
quiz.explanation: 'A bowl of soup' is correct — 'soup' is uncountable so it needs a quantifier phrase like 'a bowl of' to express quantity.

quiz.question: What does the passage recommend doing if you have a food allergy?
options: Ordering only dishes with no description on the menu
Avoiding all restaurants and cooking at home
Confirming with the server rather than relying only on the menu
Ordering the most expensive dish to ensure quality ingredients
quiz.explanation: The passage advises: 'it is always safer to confirm with the server rather than relying only on the menu description.'

listening_exercises.transcript: Let me tell you about our menu. Appetizers are small dishes you eat first, like soup or a salad. Entrées are the main dishes — those come with two sides. Sides are smaller dishes like fries, rice, or vegetables. Desserts are sweet dishes at the end, like ice cream or apple pie. Drinks are on the last page. Anything marked with a little leaf is vegetarian.
listening_exercises.question: What does the little leaf symbol mean?

listening_exercises.transcript: Menu words can be confusing at first. 'Grilled' means cooked over fire or high heat with little oil. 'Fried' means cooked in hot oil — crispy but heavier. 'Baked' or 'roasted' means cooked in an oven. 'Steamed' is cooked with hot water vapor and is usually the healthiest choice. If you're not sure what something is, just ask your server — that's completely normal.
listening_exercises.question: Which cooking method does the speaker call the healthiest?
